sections.title: Overview
blocks: A **boil (furuncle)** is a deep infection of a hair follicle that forms a small abscess. A **carbuncle** is a group of interconnected boils with several openings, and is more likely to cause systemic upset.
Most are caused by *Staphylococcus aureus*. Recurrent or severe cases raise the possibility of **Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL)-producing** *S. aureus* or **MRSA**.

sub: Common in adolescents and young adults; outbreaks in families, sports teams, prisons and the military.

ul: Deep follicular infection, usually from the patient’s own *S. aureus* carriage (nose, axillae, perineum).
Friction, shaving, sweating and minor trauma help bacteria enter.
Risk factors: **diabetes**, obesity, immunosuppression, poor hygiene, close-contact sport, crowded living, and household contacts with boils.
**Organism**: *S. aureus*, including MRSA and **Panton–Valentine leukocidin (PVL)**-producing strains (recurrent, multiple, necrotic boils).
**Risk factors**: nasal or perineal carriage, diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, eczema, friction, shaving, poor hygiene, close contact and shared towels.
**"Squeeze it to clear it"**: squeezing can spread infection; drain only when fluctuant and by a clinician.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A boil is a **follicular abscess**: neutrophils wall off staphylococci deep in the follicle.

mech.t: Neutrophils and necrotic tissue form pus; a red, hot, tender nodule becomes **fluctuant** with a yellow point.
Infection spreads through connected follicles in thick skin (back of neck, back, thighs), forming a larger mass with several heads.

histo: Dense neutrophilic abscess centred on a follicle with necrosis; Gram-positive cocci.
Swab pus for culture and sensitivity (and PVL if recurrent).

ul: A **painful, red, hot nodule** that becomes fluctuant and **points** to a yellow-white head before discharging.
Common sites: neck, face, axillae, buttocks and thighs.
**Carbuncle:** a larger, indurated area with **multiple heads**. Fever and malaise are more likely.
Surrounding cellulitis may develop.

list: **Facial boils**: Don’t squeeze; lower threshold for antibiotics and review.
**Hygiene**: Own towel, hot-wash bedding, cover the lesion, wash hands.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: **Carbuncle** or a large abscess: needs drainage.
Boil on the **central face** or near the eye.
Spreading cellulitis, fever or a systemically unwell patient.
**PVL-S. aureus suspicion:** recurrent, painful, aggressive boils, clusters in a household, gym or team, or necrotising features. Escalate to microbiology or public health.
Immunocompromised or diabetic patient with a deep infection.
Cellulitis, lymphangitis; scarring.
Bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, endocarditis (rare).
Facial 'danger triangle' boils: rare cavernous sinus thrombosis.
PVL strains: necrotising soft-tissue infection and necrotising pneumonia.
Most heal within 1–2 weeks after draining.
Recurrence is common with carriage; decolonisation helps some.

pearls: **Pus needs a way out.** Drainage is the treatment, and antibiotics are an add-on only with specific features.
‘Recurrent boils’ in the axillae or groin may be **hidradenitis suppurativa**, which follows a different pathway.
Ask about **household contacts and close-contact sport**, as PVL clusters spread this way.
Do not squeeze facial boils. Use a lower threshold for antibiotics and review.
Give practical hygiene advice: own towel, hot-wash bedding, cover the lesion, and wash hands.
